articles.title: Campus antisemitism is an America First issue. Alumni must stay in the fight.
articles.summary: A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit against Harvard, but faculty reveal ongoing antisemitic incidents in an open letter.
articles.body: Earlier this month, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit against Harvard on the grounds that the antisemitism alleged by the Justice Department was "too isolated and episodic" to show that Harvard had violated federal law. While this was a setback in the valiant effort by the federal government to address campus antisemitism, federal efforts alone will not result in meaningful change. The root of the problem is a rotten academic culture that begins in the classroom and is protected and fueled by administrators. Whoever owns the classroom owns the culture, and that culture is primarily responsible for the threat to Jewish safety today. JUDGE’S HARVARD ANTISEMITISM RULING SENDS TRUMP JUSTICE DEPARTMENT BACK TO DRAWING BOARD Recently, 170 Harvard faculty members — Jews and non-Jews alike — published an open letter highlighting antisemitic incidents that have taken place at the institution. These incidents included an Israeli undergraduate student at Harvard being "told to leave a classroom by an instructor because her being Israeli made other students uncomfortable." Other Jewish students experienced demands to "renounce Zionism" and faced ostracism when they refused. Such incidents are allowed to happen by administrators who foster a culture of impunity. DAVID MARCUS: TRANSPORTATION SECRETARY DUFFY IS RIGHT; HARVARD JUST AIN’T WHAT IT USED TO BE Antisemitism on campus is an America First issue because it is an outgrowth of the crisis in our education system. Malign actors like Qatar have embedded themselves in American academia through lavish spending that university administrators happily accept. Qatar’s foreign influence operations directed at American universities raise concerns about national security, institutional integrity, and equal protection under law. During the height of the "tentifada," the encampments and associated violations of student codes of conduct and criminal law were justified by many as displays of "free expression." Signs and screams wishing away the existence of Israel and the presence of Jewish students violated the rights of Jewish students to free expression and religious liberty around the country. DOJ SUES UCLA OVER ALLEGED ‘JUDENREIN’ CONDITIONS DURING ANTI-ISRAEL ENCAMPMENT When I was a student at George Washington University, I found inversions of justice and perversions of language. A friend of mine standing peacefully across the street holding an Israeli flag was told to leave while the tents stayed up for weeks. Later, a group known as Faculty and Staff for Justice in Palestine teamed up to defend the protesters as "peaceful." JEWISH UCLA STUDENTS BEATEN WITH STICKS, PEPPER SPRAYED AND KNOCKED OUT BY ANTI-ISRAEL CAMPUS MOB: LAWSUIT Professors who mobilize students to harass, humiliate, and ostracize their classmates are not exercising 1st Amendment rights; they are violating their academic integrity codes and using academic freedom as a cover. The public is generally not privy to the most insidious element of campus antisemitism: the syllabi. Course descriptions at Princeton and Stanford characterized the Israel-Hamas war as a Palestinian genocide. In 2025, the University of California Berkeley offered an English comparative literature course that initially referred to the Israeli military in the Palestinian territory as the "Israeli Occupying Force" and Hamas militants as "revolutionary resistance forces" standing up against colonialism and imperialism. The academic lexicon is rife with these descriptions, weaving a tapestry of lies that few dare to tear. NON-JEWISH PROFESSOR SAYS HE WAS FIRED FOR CALLING OUT HAMAS SUPPORTERS IN ONLINE POST A university is supposed to defend intellectual honesty and open minds. Instead, we find minds closing and a crisis of accountability that will continue unless administrators hold faculty to their codes, or are themselves held to account. In May 2025, I sued GW over pervasive antisemitism. The complaint details the "pipeline of hate" that begins with academic culture and spills outward. That August, the DOJ's own investigation found GW had been "deliberately indifferent" to the hostile environment facing its Jewish and Israeli students. Federal investigations and settlements provide some solace, yet they offer little remedy for what Jewish students are enduring now. Investigations take months, meaningful enforcement can take years, and a college career lasts only four. That’s why I refuse to treat commencement as the end of my role in this fight. Alumni should adopt the same mindset. I was reminded of this at the Israel on Campus Coalition's National Leadership Summit. In my remarks to students, faculty, and community leaders, I stressed that addressing antisemitism is an America First issue, and doing so requires reinfusing academic freedom with academic integrity. That is how we can inspire a new generation: a rededication to the American constitutional tradition, and a genuinely liberal education. My conversations at ICC’s Summit also underscored the importance of alumni involvement: our guidance stems from rigorous trial and error in coalition building and university engagement. Graduates are obligated to pass the baton, mentor current students, build bonds with professors, and amplify their voices so the change we yearn for is realized. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The federal government has a real role to play, but it must do so thoughtfully and with the systemic nature of the issue in mind. Federal law enforcement efforts must target classroom culture and administrative impunity that let antisemitism take root. Otherwise, the fight against antisemitism will be nothing more than an effort at pruning branches while the roots remain intact. This work is my responsibility and that of all alumni who have faced down campus antisemitism.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: House committee probes Chicago Public Schools over hiding 'gender affirmation' from parents
articles.summary: Chicago Public Schools CEO Macquline King faced House committee scrutiny over gender identity policies that allegedly hide students' transitions from parents.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — The House Committee on Education and the Workforce is demanding Chicago Public Schools (CPS) Superintendent and CEO Macquline King respond to concerns that schools are hiding information regarding students' gender transitions from parents. In a letter obtained by Fox News Digital, Committee Chair Rep. Tim Walberg, R-Mich., reached out to King in response to her testimony at a June 10 hearing titled, "Breaking Trust: Attacks on Parental Rights, Inappropriate Content, and Legal Abuses in America’s Schools." "When asked by Rep. Mary Miller, R-Ill., at the June 10 hearing about CPS’ 'socially transitioning children without parental knowledge or consent,' [King] responded, '[w]e do not hide information from parents.' However, several of CPS’s policies and resources suggest otherwise," Walberg wrote. TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS WOKE SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF HIDING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS Walberg cited CPS' interim guidelines along with a "Gender Diversity Toolkit" that prohibit staff members from disclosing a student's "transgender status or gender-nonconforming presentation" without the student's permission and clarified that parental consent is not required. The Michigan congressman expressed concerns that the vague language of the guidelines could prevent faculty from communicating with parents about students' gender identity, which could go against the Supreme Court's ruling in Mirabelli v. Bonta earlier this year. "When Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo., asked you at the June 10 hearing whether CPS had made any changes in its policies to align with the Supreme Court’s decision in Mirabelli, you deflected and failed to give a clear, direct answer. You stated that you 'hope[d]' that 'the parent, the families, the student … and the school would all be in communication,'" Walberg wrote. TRUMP DOJ CORNERS SCHOOL DISTRICT WITH 7-DAY ULTIMATUM OVER TRANS POLICY KEEPING PARENTS IN THE DARK "Notably, while you stated that CPS communicates with parents in compliance with Illinois state law, you failed to specify whether CPS complies with federal law or Mirabelli," he continued. "CPS’s policies appear to undermine the authority of parents and guardians, which the Supreme Court has stated 'have primary authority with respect to the upbringing and education of children.’" The Supreme Court ruled in Mirabelli v. Bonta that parents were likely to succeed in their claims that a California law prohibiting schools from disclosing to parents their child’s "gender identity" violated their free exercise rights under the First Amendment and their substantive due process rights under the 14th Amendment, though the case still remains in litigation at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. Meanwhile, Walberg and the committee are requesting all guidance documents, written complaints and professional development training related to gender and sexuality with a response no later than Sept. 11. LOUDOUN COUNTY PARENTS NOT 'SATISFIED' AFTER SCHOOL OFFICIALS TESTIFY ON TRANSGENDER POLICIES In a comment to Fox News Digital, Walberg added, "Parents deserve the right to know what goes on in their child’s classroom and have a say in decisions regarding their child. That is commonsense, and that right doesn’t go away at the schoolhouse door. "Yet, far too often we have seen policies that allow schools to withhold important information from parents and make decisions about a child’s name, pronouns or gender identity without their knowledge. "Our committee will always stand up for parents’ rights and defend their God-given role in their children’s lives and education."
